metadata.name: Viral hepatitis (A/B/C/E)
metadata.emergency_level: Usually routine - but acute liver failure is an emergency; some are notifiable
metadata.severity: From asymptomatic to fulminant liver failure; chronic B/C cause cirrhosis and liver cancer

overview.short_description: Inflammation of the liver caused by hepatitis viruses (A, B, C, E), ranging from a self-limiting acute illness (A, E) to chronic infection with cirrhosis and liver cancer risk (B, C).
overview.detailed_description: Viral hepatitis is diagnosed by deranged liver tests plus viral serology/nucleic acid tests. Hepatitis A and E are usually acute and self-limiting (faeco-oral). Hepatitis B and C are blood-borne and can become chronic, causing cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma - both are now highly treatable/preventable (HBV vaccine and antivirals; HCV cure with direct-acting antivirals). Primary-care roles are testing at-risk people, vaccination, recognising acute illness/red flags, and referral for chronic infection.
overview.pathophysiology: Viral infection of hepatocytes triggers immune-mediated injury; acute hepatitis causes hepatocellular necrosis (raised transaminases, sometimes jaundice); chronic infection (B/C) drives progressive fibrosis to cirrhosis and increases hepatocellular carcinoma risk.
overview.etiology: HAV and HEV (faeco-oral, contaminated food/water); HBV (blood/sexual/perinatal); HCV (blood-borne, injecting drug use). Also hepatitis D (with B).
overview.incubation_period: HAV ~2-6 weeks; HEV ~2-9 weeks; HBV ~1-6 months; HCV ~2 weeks-6 months.
overview.natural_history: A/E self-limiting; B may become chronic (higher risk if acquired at birth/infancy); C becomes chronic in most untreated. Chronic B/C: cirrhosis and HCC over years.
overview.prognosis: Excellent for A/E; chronic B controllable and C curable with modern therapy; prognosis worsens with cirrhosis.

prevalence.value: Globally very common; hundreds of millions live with chronic hepatitis B or C (WHO); higher HBV prevalence in parts of Africa/Asia.

incidence.value: Varies by virus and region; outbreaks of A/E where sanitation is poor.

mortality.value: Chronic B and C are major causes of cirrhosis, liver cancer and death worldwide (WHO).

epidemiology.seasonal_pattern: A/E outbreaks may follow contamination events.

risk_factors.lifestyle: Injecting drug use (B/C), unprotected sex (B), travel/food-water exposure (A/E).
risk_factors.smoking: Not a direct risk (worsens liver disease outcomes).
risk_factors.alcohol: Accelerates liver damage in chronic viral hepatitis.
risk_factors.pregnancy: HEV can be severe in pregnancy; perinatal HBV transmission (prevented by vaccination/antivirals).
risk_factors.travel: HAV/HEV in endemic areas; unsafe medical/tattoo procedures (B/C).
risk_factors.previous_diseases: Other blood-borne infections; chronic liver disease.

chief_complaints.complaint: Jaundice (yellow eyes/skin), dark urine, pale stools
chief_complaints.importance: Classic of acute hepatitis (often absent, esp. chronic)

symptoms.importance: Classic acute feature (often absent in chronic)
Chronic infection often silent until cirrhosis

symptoms.symptom: Confusion/drowsiness, bruising/bleeding, worsening jaundice (acute liver failure)
Signs of chronic liver disease/cirrhosis (ascites, spider naevi, splenomegaly)

negative_findings.finding: Normal LFTs and negative viral serology
negative_findings.why_important: Makes active viral hepatitis unlikely (window periods considered)

history_questions.question: Any jaundice, dark urine, pale stools, or right-upper-abdominal discomfort?
Risk factors: injecting drug use, blood transfusions/procedures, tattoos, sexual exposure, travel, contaminated food/water?
Alcohol intake and other medications/supplements?
history_questions.why_ask: Alcoholic/drug-induced liver injury differential and co-factors

history_questions.question: Any confusion, bleeding, or rapidly worsening jaundice?

physical_examination.examination: Assess for jaundice and RUQ tenderness/hepatomegaly
physical_examination.expected_finding: Jaundice; tender liver in acute hepatitis

physical_examination.examination: Signs of chronic liver disease (spider naevi, palmar erythema, ascites, splenomegaly)

physical_examination.expected_finding: Confusion/asterixis and bleeding suggest liver failure

laboratory_tests.expected_result: Raised transaminases (often very high in acute); INR/albumin reflect synthetic function

laboratory_tests.test_name: Viral serology/NAT (HAV IgM; HBsAg/anti-HBc/HBV DNA; anti-HCV/HCV RNA; HEV IgM)
laboratory_tests.indication: Identify the causative virus and chronicity

laboratory_tests.test_name: Screen for co-infection and other liver disease
laboratory_tests.indication: HIV/HBV/HCV co-infection, and exclude other causes

imaging.when_needed: Chronic hepatitis / assess cirrhosis / HCC surveillance

other_diagnostic_tests.biopsy: Liver biopsy in selected cases for staging/uncertain diagnosis
other_diagnostic_tests.pcr: HBV DNA / HCV RNA quantify viral load and confirm active infection

diagnostic_criteria.formal_criteria: Deranged liver tests (raised transaminases +/- bilirubin) with positive virus-specific markers. Chronic hepatitis B: HBsAg positive >6 months. Chronic hepatitis C: HCV RNA positive (anti-HCV indicates exposure). Acute A/E: IgM positive with a compatible acute illness.
diagnostic_criteria.diagnostic_scores: Fibrosis scores (e.g., FIB-4/APRI) and elastography stage chronic disease.

differential_diagnosis.differential_questions: How much alcohol, and any new drugs/supplements?

differential_diagnosis.differences: Obstructive LFT pattern, RUQ pain, dilated ducts
differential_diagnosis.differential_questions: Is there colicky pain with an obstructive picture?
Are viral tests negative with autoimmune/metabolic markers?
Any confusion, drowsiness, or easy bleeding?

diagnostic_questions.question: Any confusion, easy bruising/bleeding, or rapidly deepening jaundice (liver failure)?
What are the risk factors (injecting drugs, procedures, sexual exposure, travel, food/water)?

next_best_question.question: Any liver-failure features, risk factors, alcohol/drug history - and which viral markers are positive?
next_best_question.branching_logic: Liver failure -> emergency; acute A/E -> supportive + notify; chronic B/C -> refer for antiviral therapy and cancer surveillance; vaccinate contacts (A/B)

next_best_test.why: Diagnose, identify virus, and assess severity
Stage chronic disease and screen for cirrhosis/HCC

red_flags.finding: Encephalopathy, coagulopathy (raised INR), or rapidly worsening jaundice (acute liver failure)
red_flags.immediate_action: Emergency - urgent transfer to a specialist liver unit

red_flags.finding: Signs of decompensated cirrhosis (ascites, variceal bleeding, encephalopathy)

red_flags.immediate_action: Urgent specialist input (risk of severe disease)
Refer for assessment/treatment; notify per public-health rules

referral_criteria.urgent_referral: Acute liver failure; decompensated cirrhosis (emergency); severe acute hepatitis.
referral_criteria.routine_referral: All chronic hepatitis B and C for specialist assessment and antiviral treatment; abnormal fibrosis.

initial_management.supportive_care: Supportive care for acute A/E (rest, hydration, avoid hepatotoxins/alcohol); notify notifiable infections; test and vaccinate contacts where relevant.
initial_management.medications: Canonical schema 1.3 guidance: use treatment_guidance.medication_options and its history-based safety checks. Candidate classes/options (not a prescription): HBV nucleos(t)ide analogue; Pan-genotypic direct-acting antiviral; Supportive care/no antiviral. No autonomous selection or dosing is allowed. Source IDs: WHO_HBV_2024, WHO_HCV_2022.
initial_management.lifestyle_advice: Avoid alcohol, safe practices to prevent transmission, vaccination (A/B), and adherence to treatment/surveillance.
initial_management.follow_up: Specialist follow-up for chronic infection; monitor LFTs, viral load, fibrosis, and HCC surveillance in cirrhosis.
initial_management.legacy_medications_pre_v13: Acute A/E: usually supportive only. Chronic hepatitis B: antiviral therapy (e.g., tenofovir/entecavir) per specialist criteria; prevent reactivation before immunosuppression. Chronic hepatitis C: direct-acting antivirals achieve cure in most. Manage co-factors (alcohol, obesity); HCC surveillance in cirrhosis. Avoid hepatotoxic drugs.

patient_education.home_advice: Viral hepatitis is inflammation of the liver caused by a virus. Hepatitis A and E usually get better on their own with rest and fluids. Hepatitis B and C can become long-term and, over years, damage the liver - but they are now very treatable: hepatitis B can be controlled and hepatitis C can usually be cured with tablets. Avoid alcohol, get vaccinated (A and B), and take steps not to pass it on. Seek urgent help for confusion, drowsiness, easy bruising/bleeding, or deepening yellow colour.
patient_education.home_advice_ar: التهاب الكبد الفيروسي التهاب في الكبد يسبّبه فيروس. النوعان A وE يتحسّنان عادةً وحدهما بالراحة والسوائل. أما B وC فقد يصبحان مزمنَين ويُتلفان الكبد عبر السنين - لكنهما الآن قابلان جداً للعلاج: يمكن ضبط B، وغالباً يُشفى C بالأقراص. تجنّب الكحول، وخذ اللقاحات (A وB)، واتّبع وسائل عدم نقل العدوى. اطلب المساعدة العاجلة عند التشوّش أو الخمول أو سهولة الكدمات/النزيف أو ازدياد الاصفرار.
patient_education.prevention: Hepatitis A and B vaccines; safe injecting/sexual practices; safe food/water; screening at-risk groups.
patient_education.warning_signs: Confusion/drowsiness, easy bruising/bleeding, deepening jaundice, swelling of the abdomen, or vomiting blood.

prevention.vaccination: Effective vaccines for hepatitis A and B (no vaccine for C); HBV vaccination prevents infection and perinatal transmission.
prevention.lifestyle: Safe injecting/sexual practices, safe food/water, universal precautions.
prevention.screening: Screen at-risk groups for B and C (enables cure/control and prevents transmission).

evidence.evidence_level: High - HBV vaccine/antivirals and HCV direct-acting antivirals are highly effective.
evidence.guideline_strength: The main diagnosis/test and treatment direction was checked against the current guidance identified by WHO_HBV_2024, WHO_HCV_2022; see evidence_review for scope and limitations. This does not verify every legacy narrative sentence.

medication_options.when_to_consider: Only after confirmed HBV, staging and treatment-eligibility assessment
medication_options.dose_policy: Dose is not inferred from this KB; use age, weight, renal/hepatic function, pregnancy status and the current local formulary/medicine label.

use_caution_if: renal impairment, osteoporosis/bone risk, pregnancy, HIV coinfection, decompensated cirrhosis, or prior antiviral resistance
monitoring: HBV DNA, ALT, renal/bone parameters by agent, adherence and hepatocellular-carcinoma surveillance when indicated; avoid unsafe abrupt withdrawal

medication_options.clinical_note: Choice and renal/bone monitoring depend on agent and patient factors.

medication_options.when_to_consider: Confirmed active HCV infection after interaction and cirrhosis assessment
medication_options.dose_policy: Dose is not inferred from this KB; use age, weight, renal/hepatic function, pregnancy status and the current local formulary/medicine label.

avoid_if: unresolved major interaction or regimen contraindication
use_caution_if: decompensated cirrhosis, HBV coinfection/reactivation risk, pregnancy considerations, severe renal disease, prior DAA failure, or interacting acid suppressants/statins/anticonvulsants/herbals
monitoring: adherence, liver safety where indicated and sustained virologic response testing after treatment

medication_options.when_to_consider: Based on virus, severity, pregnancy and public-health guidance
